newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia PM says won't take action on detentions.
newsitem.headline: Australia PM says won't take action on detentions.

text.p: Australian Prime Minister John Howard on Sunday described as unfortunate the detention of an Australian journalist and activists by Malaysian police but said Camberra will not take action.

Malaysia began to deport on Sunday some of the 46 foreign activists detained by police after a youth group allied to the Malaysian government broke up a controversial conference in Kuala Lumpur on East Timor.
Four Australian activists were among those expelled but two journalists, including Australian Broadcasting Corporation's Catherine McGrath, were still in custody at midday on Sunday.
Howard said Australia would not take any action over the incident, noting the activists present at the conference knew it was prohibited and that they could be detained.
"I think it is an unfortunate incident but I am not going to take it beyond that," Howard told reporters in the Victoria state town of Benalla.
"When you are in another country, if you are told that something is not permitted, well you have to take notice of that or expect certain consequences," he said.
"That doesn't mean to say we agree or necessarily sanction what has happened, but we have to respect the right of other countries to conduct their affairs in the way that they see fit."
Earlier, Deputy Prime Minister and Trade Minister Tim Fischer also called the detentions unfortunate and said Foreign Minister Alexander Downer had asked for a report on the incident.
One of the activists detained was an Australian Roman Catholic bishop, the Rev. Hilton Deakin, 63, of Melbourne.
A Malaysian minister said earlier this week that the government did not want the conference to take place because it could harm bilateral ties with Indonesia.
Indonesia invaded East Timor in 1975 and now rules the territory in defiance of the United Nations.
Australia supports Indonesia's right to govern East Timor, but the government regularly comes under pressure to be more aggressive over Indonesia's human rights record.
Howard said he was satisfied the detainees would be properly treated.
He said he understood the desire of people to discuss East Timor, but they had been clearly told the meeting was prohibited.

The Australia-East Timor Association urged Downer to summon the Malaysian ambassador in Australia to explain the incident. The Association, a lobby group made up of Australians and East Timorese immigrants, has campaigned for East Timorese independence.
"More urgently, Mr Downer should call for the immediate and unconditional release of all Malaysian detainees from the conference," association spokesman Jeff Lee said in a statement.
He said a protest against the detentions would be held at the Malaysian consulate in Sydney later on Sunday.
